talks.title: International Resilience Plenary
talks.teaser: Panellists from four nations compare legislation, partnerships and incentives for building national cyber resilience.
talks.summary:
This session was the international panel at CyberUK 2025 in Manchester, chaired by the NCSC's national resilience director. It brought together senior officials from Japan, Singapore, Germany and the UK to compare how their governments strengthen cyber resilience. The panellists began by reflecting on the past year. Singapore's cyber agency head described a CrowdStrike-driven outage that was not a cyber attack but still disrupted airlines, banks and public services, which led the agency to take on resilience work alongside cyber security. Japan pointed to North Korean cryptocurrency thefts and China-linked espionage, while Germany described public attributions of attacks and the creation of a national security council.

The discussion then turned to legislation and partnership. Japan outlined its active cyber defence bill, which would add mandatory incident reporting, a single common reporting format and a stronger coordinating body, alongside a voluntary IoT security labelling scheme. Singapore said its cyber security act had been amended because it had not contemplated cloud, and that attackers target weak corporate systems regardless of how critical infrastructure is divided. It therefore moved toward partnership and voluntary reporting, and reported that its labelling scheme gave firms a market differentiator. Germany described NIS2 expanding reporting obligations from about 4,500 companies to an estimated 29,000. The panel also acknowledged that measuring resilience is hard, and that uptake of schemes such as Cyber Essentials is one practical proxy.

In closing, the panellists stressed mainstreaming cyber security at every level, joint attribution and public-private partnership, and treating security as a shared international effort rather than only a compliance burden.

talks.title: Technology Plenary
talks.teaser: Argues that market incentives must reward secure products, and that buyers and governments need to fix the supply chain.
talks.summary:
The NCSC chief technology officer, Ollie White, opened by framing the scale of the problem. Technology suppliers behind critical systems have grown from a few dozen firms to tens of thousands, and edge and security devices still ship with vulnerability classes he called unforgivable. He said AI is making some bug classes easier to find and exploit, and that the post-quantum migration will be a large change programme. As an example of secure foundations taking hold, he cited the NHS, whose passkey use grew from a few thousand logins in its first month to over a million users a month without marketing.

He then argued that technical debt must be measured in terms boards understand, and that systems with growing autonomy will never be fully understood, so resilience and observability matter more. The privileged access workstation model was offered as an architectural principle that raises attacker costs. A panel of Emma Smith (Vodafone), Stuart McKenzie (Mandiant, part of Google), Bridget Walsh (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security) and Ben (Sage) then debated whether vendors are rewarded for security. Panellists agreed buyers hold real power and that customers repeat the same testing, while guidance, certification and insurance can set baselines. They disagreed on penalties and on whether MFA should be included in base prices.

The closing call to action was to simplify and align supply chain requirements, to state clearly what security a buyer needs, and to standardise how vendors describe what they do and do not do. Ollie said NCSC would work with international partners on minimum transparency standards.

talks.title: Ecosystem Plenary
talks.teaser: Covers Akamai's view of east-west API risk, then a panel on why basic cyber hygiene and Cyber Essentials still fall short.
talks.summary:
Charlie Garrell, Akamai's CTO, opens by describing how internal services constantly talk to one another, often through APIs with little authentication, creating a large attack surface. He splits the response into two questions: which processes should be allowed to communicate at all, which he tackles with micro-segmentation, and whether the content they send is legitimate, which API security addresses through behavioural analysis. He also covers bot traffic, DDoS and DNS attacks, treats generative AI as an advanced API that needs an AI firewall, and argues for moving security checks earlier into developer workflows.

The second half is a panel chaired by Felicity Oswald of the NCSC on whether organisations are getting the basics of cyber security right. Panellists from Australia's ASD, the UK's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, BAE Systems and the Information Commissioner's Office all answer no. They describe patchy adoption, legacy systems that are never retired, and missing logs. BAE's global CISO explains how making Cyber Essentials a condition of doing business internally led to a sharp fall in vulnerabilities on certified systems. Australia's Essential Eight shows that mandation can help unlock funding but can also encourage tick-box compliance.

The closing discussion covers regulation, pressure on suppliers through procurement, and the ICO's advice to learn from published investigations and weigh the cost of a breach against preventive controls. The panel agrees that cyber security is a whole-organisation responsibility and that unglamorous basics should come before new tools.

talks.title: Richard Horne’s keynote address at CYBERUK 2025
talks.teaser: The NCSC chief outlines the UK's cyber threat picture, resilience priorities and the role of AI in defence.
talks.summary:
Overview: Richard Horne delivers the CYBERUK 2025 keynote in Manchester, framing cybersecurity as a contest rather than a problem to control, with updates on nation-state threats facing the UK.

Key Topics: Cybersecurity as an ongoing contest between opposing players; NCSC Manchester presence; Russian cyber espionage against Ukraine; Iranian targeting of UK firms; North Korean IT worker infiltration; and persistent ransomware threats.

Technical Details: Horne provides threat landscape updates covering Russian, Iranian, and North Korean activity alongside criminal ransomware operations. He emphasizes that organizations cannot control every point but must compete effectively in the cyber contest.

Takeaways: Defenders must adopt a contest mindset rather than seeking total control. Understanding nation-state motivations and capabilities is essential for UK organizations building resilience.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Richard Horne, Chief Executive Officer of the UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), delivers the opening keynote address at CYBERUK 2025 in Manchester. Framing cybersecurity through the metaphor of a tennis match, Horne emphasizes that organizations cannot completely control the external threat landscape or eliminate all incidents, but must rigorously "control the controllables" through foundational hygiene, resilience, and pre-engineered recovery capabilities. Horne reviews the UK's operational threat landscape—highlighting nation-state threats from China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea alongside persistent ransomware—and details national defense initiatives across Active Cyber Defence (ACD), post-quantum migration, and artificial intelligence integration.

Key Topics:
- The cybersecurity "contest": shifting operational focus toward controlling controllable variables and building rapid-recovery resilience
- Geopolitical nation-state threat landscape: Chinese systemic scale, Russian sabotage and gray-zone operations, Iranian cyber espionage, and North Korean IT worker revenue generation
- National security initiatives: NCSC incident response metrics (>200 incidents managed), Active Cyber Defence (ACD), and the "Share and Defend" ISP blocking partnership
- Emerging technological frontiers: the double-edged sword of AI in cyber defense/offense and the NCSC post-quantum cryptography migration roadmap

Technical Details:
Horne provides high-level telemetry regarding the UK threat environment, noting that the NCSC managed over 200 security incidents between September 2024 and mid-2025, including twice as many nationally significant incidents compared to the prior year. Addressing state adversaries operating in the "gray zone" between peace and overt conflict, Horne identifies the Chinese Communist Party as the "pacing threat," leveraging a unified strategic ecosystem of capability, legislation, and vast data access. Drawing on assessments with MI5 and the National Protective Security Authority (NPSA), Horne highlights Russian intelligence services executing hybrid cyber-physical sabotage and criminal proxy operations on UK streets, assessing with near certainty that Russian cyber espionage against Ukraine and Western allies will persist during any potential ceasefire negotiations.

The keynote outlines additional persistent threats: heightened cyber espionage campaigns emanating from Iranian state actors, fraudulent North Korean IT workers masquerading as freelance third-country contractors to funnel revenue to the DPRK regime, and pervasive ransomware extortion. In response to ransomware, Horne points to the Home Office consultation on ransomware and stresses that enterprise architectures must eliminate the economic incentive of attacker business models by ensuring systems can fully restore without paying ransoms.

On defensive modernization, Horne details NCSC's Active Cyber Defence (ACD) program and the "Share and Defend" initiative, which shares malicious domain intelligence with UK Internet Service Providers (ISPs) in near real-time, blocking millions of attempted malicious connections from end-users at network scale. Operating within GCHQ alongside the National Cyber Force (NCF) for offensive disruption and the National Crime Agency (NCA) for law enforcement action, NCSC reinforces that offense is vital to national defense. Horne also highlights NCSC's role as the National Technical Authority, referencing their March roadmap for post-quantum cryptography migration to counter future quantum decryption threats, while urging organizations to embrace defensive AI for machine-speed threat elimination and secure-by-design code generation.

Key Takeaways:
Organizations must accept that complete prevention in complex, interconnected supply chains is unachievable; true security lies in architecting environments that minimize blast radius and ensure rapid, validated system recovery without paying ransoms. Enterprises should implement baseline hygiene standards like Cyber Essentials and follow the DSIT Code of Practice for Cyber Security Governance to hold senior executives accountable. Finally, technical teams must proactively begin planning migrations to post-quantum cryptographic standards and adopt machine-speed AI defensive tooling to avoid falling on the wrong side of an emerging technological divide.
